questions.prompt: What role do identifiers play in a Cangjie program?

choices.text: They are compiler directives that control optimization flags.
They are user-defined names given to program elements like variables, functions, and types.
They are numeric literals stored directly in CPU registers.
They are punctuation marks that mark the termination of statements.

questions.explanation: In Cangjie, an identifier is simply a name you choose for program elements—such as a variable (totalScore), a function (calculateTax), a struct, or a package.

questions.prompt: Which of the following characters is permitted as the first character of an ordinary Cangjie identifier?

choices.text: A digit from 0 to 9 (e.g., 3count)
A hyphen (e.g., -total)
An English letter or underscore (e.g., count or _count)
A dollar sign (e.g., $price)

questions.explanation: Ordinary identifiers in Cangjie must begin with either a letter (ASCII or Unicode) or an underscore (_). They can never begin with a digit or special symbols like - or $.

questions.prompt: Why does the Cangjie compiler reject the declaration let 2ndPlayer = "Alice"?

choices.text: Variable names must contain at least 10 characters.
Ordinary identifiers cannot start with a numeric digit.
The word Player is a reserved system keyword.
String literals cannot be assigned to variables containing numbers.

questions.explanation: When the compiler encounters a leading 2, it expects a numeric literal rather than an identifier name. A valid alternative would be player2 or secondPlayer.

questions.prompt: Which characters are allowed in an ordinary Cangjie identifier after its first character?

choices.text: Letters, digits, and underscores (_)
Any keyboard character, including spaces and periods
Letters and punctuation symbols like @, #, and !
Digits and mathematical operators like + and *

questions.explanation: After the initial letter or underscore, an identifier can include any combination of letters, numbers, and underscores. Punctuation marks (like #, @, -, or spaces) are invalid.

questions.prompt: Suppose you declare var userScore = 10 and var UserScore = 20 in the same scope. How does Cangjie treat these two names?

choices.text: The compiler merges them into a single variable holding the average value.
Cangjie is case-sensitive, so userScore and UserScore are two completely distinct variables.
Cangjie ignores letter casing and triggers a duplicate variable error.
The lowercase version is automatically overwritten by the uppercase version.

questions.explanation: Cangjie is strictly case-sensitive. userScore, UserScore, and USERSCORE refer to separate identifiers, though keeping names distinct in meaning is recommended for clean code.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to declare let class = "Science" in Cangjie without special syntax?

choices.text: The compiler accepts it and infers the type as a string.
The compiler raises a syntax error because class is a reserved language keyword.
The variable is automatically converted into an object-oriented class definition.
The compiler creates an anonymous struct named Science.

questions.explanation: Words like class, let, func, and struct are reserved keywords with built-in meanings in Cangjie grammar. You cannot use them directly as ordinary variable names.

questions.prompt: If you need to name an identifier using a reserved keyword (for example, when matching an external API field named var), how does Cangjie allow you to write it?

choices.text: Enclose the keyword in double quotes: "var"
Prefix the keyword with an ampersand: &var
Enclose the keyword in backticks as a raw identifier: `var`
Add a trailing exclamation mark: var!

questions.explanation: Cangjie supports raw identifiers using backticks (e.g., `var` or `class`). This instructs the compiler to treat the enclosed token strictly as an identifier rather than as a language keyword.

questions.prompt: In Cangjie, what is the role of a standalone single underscore _?

choices.text: It is a wildcard or discard placeholder used to ignore unneeded values or patterns.
It automatically prints the previous evaluation result to the terminal.
It is an ordinary variable name that can be read anywhere in a function.
It declares a global variable accessible across all packages.

questions.explanation: A single underscore _ is a wildcard identifier. You use it when you intentionally want to ignore a return value, tuple element, or pattern match result. Because it represents a discarded value, you cannot read from _ like a regular variable.

questions.prompt: According to standard Cangjie naming conventions, which casing style is recommended for variable and function names versus types (such as classes and structs)?

choices.text: Variables and functions use lowerCamelCase; types use UpperCamelCase (PascalCase).
Variables use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE; types use lower_snake_case.
All names must be written in lowercase with hyphens (kebab-case).
Functions use UpperCamelCase; types and variables use all uppercase.

questions.explanation: Standard Cangjie style follows idiomatic modern practice: types (classes, structs, enums, interfaces) use UpperCamelCase (e.g., StudentRecord), while variables, functions, and parameters use lowerCamelCase (e.g., calculateTotal).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a valid ordinary identifier that compiles without errors in Cangjie?

choices.text: total-amount
_max_retry_count
3rdAttempt
user name

questions.explanation: _max_retry_count is valid because it begins with an underscore and contains only letters, digits, and underscores. The others are invalid: total-amount contains a hyphen (subtraction operator), 3rdAttempt starts with a digit, and user name contains a space.
